summary.text: A molecular cloud is an interstellar cloud dense and large enough for molecules to form, most commonly molecular hydrogen.
Molecular hydrogen is hard to detect, so astronomers use carbon monoxide, which is much easier to detect, to trace the clouds where stars form.
Inside a cloud, denser clumps of dust and gas are where star formation begins if gravitational forces are strong enough to make them collapse.

facts.label: Also called
facts.value: A stellar nursery, when stars are forming within

facts.label: Milky Way volume
facts.value: Under one percent of the interstellar medium, yet densest

items.prompt: You cannot see a friend's face in a dark room, so you look for the glow of their phone instead. In the same spirit, what do astronomers look for to find hard-to-see molecular hydrogen?

options.label: Carbon monoxide, which is far easier to detect
Visible starlight shining out of the cloud's core
The glow of hydrogen fusing inside the cloud
Dust that glows white when it is heated

items.explain: Molecular hydrogen is hard to detect, so carbon monoxide, which is easier to detect, is most often used to determine its presence.

items.prompt: Why does molecular hydrogen stay nearly invisible to direct observation, despite being so abundant?

options.label: It is too hot and gives off only X-rays
Its symmetrical shape gives it weak rotational and vibrational modes
It exists for only a few moments before it breaks apart
Its mass is too large to emit any radio signal

items.explain: Because the H₂ molecule is symmetrical, it has weak rotational and vibrational modes, which makes it virtually invisible to direct observation.

items.prompt: Inside a cloud, one patch is much denser than its surroundings, full of dust and gas. When does that patch become the beginning of a star?

options.label: As soon as it becomes warm enough to start glowing
Whenever a radio signal is detected from that patch
Only after its gas has been fully ionized
When gravity is strong enough to collapse its dust and gas

items.explain: Clumps are the beginning of star formation if gravitational forces are sufficient to cause the dust and gas to collapse.

items.prompt: Molecular gas sits mostly in the Milky Way's spiral arms, and material takes about 10 million years to pass through an arm. What does that suggest about how long molecular clouds last?

options.label: They survive for billions of years once they form
They never break apart, they only grow
They form and break apart in under about 10 million years
They drift out of the arms soon after they form

items.explain: Because the gas occurs mainly in the arms, the clouds must form and dissociate on a timescale shorter than the 10 million years it takes material to cross an arm.

items.prompt: In some regions, atoms are packed densely enough in a large cloud that they can pair up. What do they most commonly form?

options.label: Molecular hydrogen, written H₂
Pairs of helium atoms bound by gravity
Chains of dust grains
Single ionized hydrogen atoms

items.explain: A molecular cloud is dense and large enough to permit the formation of molecules, most commonly molecular hydrogen.

items.prompt: A map of the Milky Way shows where molecular gas is richest. Which pattern does it follow?

options.label: Random scatter, with no pattern at all
The galaxy's spiral arms
The orbit of the Sun
A line along the galaxy's outer edge

items.explain: Large-scale CO maps show that the position of this gas correlates with the spiral arms of the galaxy.
